title: The mustard seed
hookLine: Kisa Gotami seeks medicine for her dead child from a house where no one has died (Therigatha commentary)

cards: Right after a loss, the world keeps moving, and that can feel wrong. People say things that don't help. A grieving person may go looking for the one thing, the one call or the one answer, that would undo it.
In ancient India, a young mother named Kisa Gotami went looking for exactly that. The Buddhist texts remember her walk. It's a tender story, so i'll go slowly.

teach.b: Her name means something like Gotami the thin one. The story is told in the old Buddhist commentaries, on the poems of the early nuns and on the Dhammapada. She married and had a little boy.
When he was just old enough to walk, he fell sick and died, and she couldn't accept it. She carried him on her hip from house to house in the city, asking everyone for medicine for her son.
People turned away, or thought she had lost her mind. Finally someone sent her to the Buddha. He didn't argue.
He didn't explain. He said: yes, I can help.
Bring me a mustard seed, from a house where no one has ever died. Mustard seed was in every kitchen, the easiest thing in the world to ask for. So she went.
At the first house: of course, take some. But we lost our father last year. At the next house, a daughter.
Then a husband, a grandmother, a baby. Every door would give her the seed. No door could give her the seed she needed.
Somewhere along that street, the story says, she understood. Death hadn't singled her out.
It was in every house. She laid her son down, gently, came back to the Buddha, and later became a nun; her own verses are kept among the poems of the early nuns.
He taught her not by arguing, but first with a walk, and a street of neighbors who knew her grief from the inside, and only then with a few words.
She just wasn't alone in it anymore.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Kisa Gotami in teaching on impermanence and grief, and she is honored as one of the enlightened nuns whose verses are kept in the Therigatha.

o: a grieving mother who later became a nun
a royal cook famed for her rice dishes
a village healer who gave out mustard seed

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha gave her a long sermon about death
he sent her on a walk, asking for a mustard seed.
mustard seed was hard to find
it was in every kitchen, and every house offered it.
Kisa Gotami's own verses are kept in the Therigatha
the poems of the early nuns, where she is remembered as awakened.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a young mother brings her dead son and begs you for medicine. what do you do?
o: explain gently that nothing can be done
ask her for a mustard seed from a house where no one has died
tell her to stop grieving and let go
games.why: he asks for a mustard seed from a house untouched by death. every house offers the seed; none is untouched. on that walk, she understands.

practice: If there's someone you've lost, let them come to mind gently, a face, a voice, a small ordinary moment, and if tears come, let them; if no one comes to mind, hold someone who's grieving.
Then think of the other houses, on your street, in your town, in the world, where someone is remembering too, right now: your grief is yours, and it's also in good company.
And if grief ever gets too heavy to carry alone, reach out: in the US you can call or text 988 at any hour, and wherever you are, help is there.

wordCard.voice: Kisa Gotami. A young mother whose grief sent her searching for a mustard seed from a home untouched by death.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: kisa means thin or lean; Gotami is her family name.

carryVoice: Your line: no house without it. A small, kind word is enough. Day seventy-five, gently.
